segments.narration: Runners suffered near-fatal exhaustion, dehydration, and even poisoning from experimental stimulants during the scorching 1904 St. Louis Olympic marathon.
Athletes battled choking dust clouds, severe dehydration, and trainers who dosed them with strychnine as an experimental stimulant. Yet the cheating was even wilder than the medicine.
One frontrunner actually hitched a ride in a car for much of the race, waved at spectators, and tried to claim the gold medal before officials caught him.
The true victor crossed the line while actively hallucinating, hoisted upright by trainers who carried him over the line while he shuffled his feet.
Miraculously, no one died on that brutal course, but how did judges ever let a race with zero water stations happen in the first place?

grounding.subject: 1904 Olympic marathon
grounding.article: Athletics at the 1904 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon

accuracy_flags.claim: Nineteen runners nearly died from consuming a toxic mixture of raw egg whites and strychnine during the 1904 Olympic marathon.
accuracy_flags.note: Only Thomas Hicks was given strychnine and brandy/raw eggs by his trainers, and out of 32 starters, 14 finished, but the text does not state that 19 runners nearly died from it (William Garcia suffered internal injuries from dust, and others dropped out from exhaustion/dehydration).

accuracy_flags.claim: Fred Lorz rode in a car for eleven miles before jogging across the finish line to claim first place.
accuracy_flags.note: Fred Lorz dropped out after nine miles (not eleven) and hitched a ride until the car broke down at the 19th mile, meaning he rode for about 10 miles, not 11.

accuracy_flags.claim: Marathon organizers provided only a single well of water along a grueling thirty-two kilometer dirt course.
accuracy_flags.note: The course length was 24 miles 1500 yards (roughly 40 km, not 32 km), and the single well was at about the halfway mark.

accuracy_flags.claim: The heat and dust kicked up by passing spectator automobiles triggered near-fatal respiratory distress in the athletes.
accuracy_flags.note: The dust clouds were kicked up by cars carrying race officials (ahead of and behind the runners), not spectator automobiles.
